name: How much contingency should I keep for an older home remodel?

mainEntity.name: What percentage of the budget should be reserved for surprises in a 1950s or older house?
mainEntity.text: What percentage of the budget should be reserved for surprises in a 1950s or older house?

acceptedAnswer.text: Older homes often reveal hidden conditions that are not obvious at the bid stage, so a contingency reserve is essential. A common planning range is 10% to 20% of the construction budget, with the higher end used when the home is older, has not been updated in decades, or is likely to need major structural or systems work. The contingency protects against issues like outdated wiring, damaged plumbing, termite activity, water intrusion, and unpermitted modifications. If the remodel is luxury-level or involves a full gut renovation, the reserve may need to be higher because the work exposes more unknown conditions. The best way to use contingency funds is to treat them as a true backup, not part of the base design budget. That way, the project can absorb surprises without sacrificing core scope. Homeowners should also ask the contractor how change orders are approved so contingency spending stays controlled.
acceptedAnswer.description: For older homes, many homeowners keep a contingency of about 10% to 20% of the construction budget. Homes with uncertain conditions, hidden damage, or major system replacement may need an even larger reserve.
